Meta Expert: Cross-Layer Expert Sharing for Storage- and Retrieval-Efficient MoE

Ermo Hua Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Xiangyu Hong Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Baiting Wu Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Che Jiang Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Haozheng Hou Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Yicheng Gu Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Hanjing Wang Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Qirui Zeng Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Ming Zhang Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Ning Ding Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Qipeng Guo Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Youbang Sun Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Biqing Qi Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory    Bowen Zhou Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory
Abstract

As model parameters scale up, sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches have become essential for model scaling. However, mainstream models currently adopt hierarchical architectures, where experts in different layers, although topologically independent, exhibit substantial similarity and redundancy in their stored content. Compared to the hierarchically arranged Local Expert in existing mainstream models, we hypothesize that inter-layer shared Meta Expert hold greater potential. To this end, we conduct a multi-dimensional empirical comparison between Local and Meta Experts, and find that models incorporating Meta Experts exhibit lower parameter redundancy, together with lower cross-entropy loss and higher downstream task accuracy. With the activated quantity and the expert granularity held fixed, our model matches the performance of Vanilla MoE using only 70–80% of the experts, substantially improving the model’s scaling potential. Beyond removing inter-layer redundancy among experts and improving information storage efficiency, our theoretical analysis further shows that, compared with Local Experts, Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible residual pathways, thereby improving information retrieval efficiency.

1 Introduction

In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have gradually approached or even surpassed human-level ability in general text, mathematics, and code (Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI et al., 2024). This progress owes much to the increasing scale of model parameters and training data: intelligence has been improved substantially as both factors grow (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022b).

To enable ever-larger models, parameter sparsification has become an important approach (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022; Muennighoff et al., 2025). As the module that accounts for the vast majority of model parameters, the feed-forward network was originally a densely computed block. (Vaswani et al., 2017a). However, as model size grows, such dense computation gradually becomes prohibitively expensive, creating efficiency bottlenecks for both training and inference (Lepikhin et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2022). Meanwhile, although feed-forward networks are densely computed, only a sparse subset of parameters is actually activated for a given token during its forward pass (Li et al., 2023; Mirzadeh et al., 2024); the remaining inactive parameters still participate in the computation, leading to substantial waste.

To address this, researchers have proposed designing feed-forward networks with a natively sparse-activation structure, most notably the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022). MoE splits the feed-forward network into multiple sub-networks along the intermediate dimension and routes each token to only a limited number of them before computation. This design endows the model with a large total parameter count while ensuring that each token’s forward pass computation uses only a small fraction of parameters, reconciling scale with efficiency.

With the advent of increasingly sparse MoE models, parameter efficiency along the width dimension has been steadily improved (Dai et al., 2024). In this work, however, we ask how parameter efficiency can be improved along the depth dimension (Raposo et al., 2024). On the one hand, interpretability studies suggest that feed-forward networks store relatively static knowledge (Geva et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2022), and that different layers may store similar knowledge, suggesting nontrivial redundancy across layers (Meng et al., 2022; Takase and Kiyono, 2023; Fan et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2025; Men et al., 2025). On the other hand, Looped Transformers reuse the same parameters across recurrent applications of a block (Dehghani et al., 2018; Giannou et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2019; Csordás et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026a),and recent work shows that this design can attain the reasoning performance of much larger models with far fewer parameters (Bae et al., 2025; Saunshi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). This benefit, however, comes with additional recursions and greater serial depth, incurring higher computational and latency costs.

To balance parameter storage efficiency and computational cost, this work explores the potential of another Parameter Loop scheme — Cross-Layer Expert Sharing. Unlike Looped Transformers, which keep the total parameters of each layer unchanged but increase the number of recursions, we aim to keep the number of recursions unchanged while increasing the candidate experts of each layer, and use the sparse activation of MoE to keep both the activated parameters and the computation per layer unchanged. We refer to the experts shared across layers as Meta Experts, and the layer-private experts in the conventional design as Local Experts.

Our experiments show that, compared with the Local Expert of hierarchical architectures, Meta Experts reduce parameter redundancy and achieve lower cross-entropy loss together with higher downstream task accuracy. At a fixed number of activated experts and expert granularity, our model achieves comparable performance to Vanilla MoE with only 70% as many experts, indicating a substantially higher effective capacity per parameter. Further analysis reveals another reason why cross-layer expert sharing is effective: Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible paths for storage and retrieval. Compared with hierarchical architectures, cross-layer expert sharing implicitly provides more flexible residual connections: beyond the forward residual connections, it introduces a backward residual connection at the activation level—one that operates within a single forward pass and is therefore absent from existing models.

Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) A systematic analysis of the effect of Meta Experts on model performance, covering their activation and total-number ratios among all experts, their presence in every layer, and their partial hierarchical organization. Although these configurations moderately affect performance, Meta Experts consistently bring significant improvements. (2) An explanation of why Meta Experts are effective from the perspective of residual connections. By comparing the forward hidden-state updates and the backward parameter updates of models with and without Meta Experts, we show that this design grants shallow and deep layers bidirectional access to representations across depth, enabling more flexible information retrieval.

2 Meta Expert

A MoE-based Transformer layer ll consists of an attention block and a MoE block (Fig 2.(a)). The MoE block contains a layer-specific router RlR_{l} and NN Local Experts {ϕe​(⋅,θle)}e=0N−1\{\phi_{e}(\cdot;\theta_{l}^{e})\}_{e=0}^{N-1}, both of which are initialized and accessed independently across layers. Given the hidden state x^l\hat{x}_{l} of a token entering the MoE block, the router computes gating scores from its logits and selects the top-kk experts belonging to the current layer to process the token:

yl=∑e∈topk⁡(Rl,x^l)Rl​(x^l)e​ϕe​(x^l,θle).y_{l}\;=\;\sum_{e\in\mathrm{topk}(R_{l},\hat{x}_{l})}R_{l}(\hat{x}_{l})_{e}\,\phi_{e}(\hat{x}_{l};\theta_{l}^{e}). (1)

In a model built purely from Meta Experts (Fig 2.(b)), the layer-private MoE blocks are replaced with a single shared block: one router RR and one pool of MM experts {ϕe​(⋅,θe)}e=0M−1\{\phi_{e}(\cdot;\theta^{e})\}_{e=0}^{M-1} could be activated by every layer:

yl=∑e∈topk⁡(R,x^l)R​(x^l)e​ϕe​(x^l,θe),y_{l}\;=\;\sum_{e\in\mathrm{topk}(R,\hat{x}_{l})}R(\hat{x}_{l})_{e}\,\phi_{e}(\hat{x}_{l};\theta^{e}), (2)

3 Empirical Comparison between Meta and Local Experts

To systematically analyze the effect of Meta Experts on model performance, we start from a model with only Local Experts and incorporate Meta Experts in various forms, comparing model capabilities with and without them.

3.1 Setups

Core Variables. We consider two types of relationship between Meta Experts and Local Experts: (1) the quantitative relationship: the ratio of their total numbers within the whole model and their activated numbers within each layer (See Fig 3.(a)); (2) the topological relationship: whether every layer contains both Meta and Local Experts (See Fig 3.(b)), and whether the Meta Experts are also hierarchically organized (See Fig 3.(c)).

Common Settings. During the experiments, we first sweep all the variables on a 2B-A0.5B model, and then select the relatively better-performing configurations for the scaling ladder experiments. Throughout the experiments, we keep the total number of experts and the total activation count fixed, which indirectly ensures that different models have similar FLOPs, enabling a fairer comparison. When comparing models at different FLOPs, all models adopt the training-optimal configuration of the Vanilla MoE structure, rather than a configuration tuned specifically for our design. Detailed experimental setups can be found in A.3

Metrics. In addition to cross-entropy loss and downstream task accuracy, we introduce an expert-redundancy metric as a complementary perspective for analyzing expert specialization under different architectural settings. It allows us to examine how expert topology affects the overlap among learned expert functions. The exact training configurations and the definition of the redundancy metric are deferred to Appendix A.2.

3.2 Meta/Local Experts’ ratio

We first study the effect of the ratio between the total numbers of Meta Experts and Local Experts, and of their activation ratio within each layer, on model performance.

Settings. For the total-number ratio, we consider Meta Expert proportions of 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100%; for the activation ratio, we consider proportions of 25%, 50%, or 75%. For concreteness, consider a two-layer model with 256 experts in total and 8 experts activated per layer. A Meta/Local number ratio of 75% then corresponds to 192 Meta Experts, shared across all layers, and 32 Local Experts per layer; an activation ratio of 75% corresponds to activating 6 Meta Experts and 2 Local Experts per layer.

Pilot Experiments (Fig 4). The results show that, at any activation ratio, a higher total-parameter proportion of Meta Experts consistently leads to lower loss and redundancy; meanwhile, allocating a higher activation ratio to Meta Experts also helps reduce the loss. Taken together, these observations attest to the effectiveness of Meta Experts. On the other hand, while assigning a higher activation ratio to Local Experts is detrimental to the loss, it does help reduce the redundancy among experts. This suggests that, compared with Meta Experts, Local Experts—each of which is activated in only one layer under the traditional architecture—may be harder to train sufficiently, and this under-training may give rise to redundancy.

Scaling Ladder (Fig 5). Given that activating 4 Meta Experts and 4 Local Experts per layer yields consistently better loss, we hold this activation ratio fixed and conduct a full scaling-ladder validation across the total-number ratios of 25%/50%/75%. The results confirm that, although still slightly worse than the Pure-Meta-Expert setting, the 75%75\% ratio achieves the best performance over all Partial-Meta settings at every compute budget, in terms of both cross-entropy loss and expert redundancy. Considering that a model with only Meta Experts may suffer from training instability, we adopt the 75% configuration in all subsequent experiments.

3.3 Meta/Local Experts’ topology

We next investigate the effect of the topology of Meta/Local Experts on model performance. On the one hand, we explore whether every layer should include Meta Experts; on the other hand, we explore whether the Meta Experts should themselves be partially hierarchically organized.

Settings. On the one hand, we consider variants in which Local Experts are used exclusively, with no Meta Experts introduced at all: either in only the first 1, 2, 4, or 8 layers of the model, in only the last 1, 2, 4, or 8 layers, or in both the first and the last 1, 2, or 4 layers. On the other hand, we consider partitioning the Meta Experts into 2, 4, or 8 sub-pools, which are then accessed in a looped manner—either in a chunked or an interleaved fashion.

Pilot Experiments (Fig 6). It can be observed that both operations—introducing Local-Experts-only layers, and organizing the Meta Experts hierarchically so as to mimic the topology of Local Experts—generally incur a loss degradation, which further demonstrates the positive role of Meta Experts in model performance. Notably, under a lighter degree of intervention, the loss slightly improves: for example, when only the first two and the last two layers are restricted to Local Experts, or when the Meta Experts are looped only twice. This suggests, on the one hand, that experts in the shallowest and deepest layers serve more differentiated functions, with essentially no mutual redundancy between these layers—a conclusion also supported by the expert redundancy measurements. On the other hand, mildly hierarchical Meta Experts help improve the model capability slightly; hierarchy, however, introduces a certain amount of expert redundancy, and why this redundancy does not translate into a higher loss remains an open question for further investigation.

Scaling Ladder (Fig 7). Compared with other configurations, introducing Local-Experts-only layers at both the shallow and the deep ends, and partitioning the Meta Experts into sub-pools in an interleaved manner, yield consistently better results; we therefore supplement full scaling-ladder validation under these two configurations. The results show that, at every FLOPs configuration, the best performance is achieved by using Local Experts exclusively in the first two and the last two layers, together with partitioning the Meta Experts into 2 sub-pools. We also observe that, as the model becomes deeper, using more Local-Experts-only layers and a larger hierarchy of Meta Experts likewise exhibits better results. This suggests, on the one hand, that the proportion of specialized shallow and deep layers relative to the total number of layers may remain roughly constant as model depth changes; on the other hand, deeper models also call for a larger hierarchical expert topology; the Local Experts of the Vanilla model, however, are overly hierarchical, and can therefore only achieve suboptimal results.

Overall Comparison (Fig 1 & 8) We combine the best configurations identified in each ablation and find that the combined model consistently outperforms every individual configuration in terms of loss. Building on this best configuration, we further reduce the number of Meta Experts and find that, compared with the Vanilla model, models with Meta Experts save approximately 20–30% of the experts (or 15–25% of the parameters, since other modules also account for a certain fraction of the parameters), with the advantage becoming more pronounced as the model size grows.

3.4 Downstream Performance of Meta Experts-based Model

For a more comprehensive comparison, beyond cross-entropy loss, we further compare the downstream task capabilities of different configurations through training at a larger scale.

Settings. Using the best configuration identified in each of the ablation studies above, we train 6B-A1.6B models for 200B tokens and evaluate their downstream task performance. We compare five variants: the Vanilla baseline (Vanilla MoE, Local Experts only), the MR75 model, which activates Meta Experts at a 75% meta ratio, and three topological refinements of MR75—MR75 + Loop2, which partitions the Meta Experts into two interleaved sub-pools; MR75 + F2L2, which restricts the first two and last two layers to Local Experts only; and their combination, MR75 + F2L2 + Loop2. All variants use the same total number of experts, per-layer activation budget, and training recipe, ensuring that performance differences are attributable to the expert topology. We evaluate the models across a diverse set of benchmarks covering complementary capabilities: world knowledge and factual question answering in both English (MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021)) and Chinese (C-Eval (Huang et al., 2023) and CMMLU (Li et al., 2024)); multi-step and commonsense reasoning (BBH (Kazemi et al., 2025) with chain-of-thought and OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018)); and open-ended, knowledge-intensive generation (TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017)).

Results. Table 1 reports the downstream performance of the five expert-topology variants after training on 200B tokens. Due to the limited training budget, different Meta Expert variants exhibit advantages across different datasets, highlighting the need for larger-scale scaling experiments, but incorporating Meta Experts consistently outperform the vanilla baseline.

4 Meta Experts as Bidirectional Residual Pathways

Consider a stack of LL MoE layers with hidden size HH. Writing xlx_{l} for the residual stream entering the MoE sub-layer of layer ll, x^l=RMSNorm⁡(xl)\hat{x}_{l}=\mathrm{RMSNorm}(x_{l}), and γ\gamma for the residual scaling coefficient, the sub-layer updates the stream as

xl+1=xl+γ​Eθl​(x^l,Rl),x_{l+1}\;=\;x_{l}\;+\;\gamma\,E_{\theta_{l}}(\hat{x}_{l};\,R_{l}), (3)

where EθlE_{\theta_{l}} is an expert block of NN SwiGLU experts, each with parameter dimension dd, RlR_{l} is the router, and top-kk routing activates kk experts per token. In a layer-wise MoE, θl\theta_{l} and RlR_{l} are layer-private; in Meta Experts, a single block θ\theta and router RR are learned once and shared by all layers.

4.1 Layer-wise MoE.

Forward (read). The expert of layer ll injects its output into the residual stream at layer ll (Eq. equation 3) and propagates only forward: hidden state xmx_{m} can contain layer ll’s content only if l<ml<m, and even then only as a frozen component, because the readout operator of layer mm (Eθm,RmE_{\theta_{m}},R_{m}) differs from the write operator of layer ll (Eθl,RlE_{\theta_{l}},R_{l}).

Training (write). The residual connection does run backward as a gradient highway: the adjoint x¯l=∂ℒ/∂xl\bar{x}_{l}=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x_{l} inherits x¯l+1\bar{x}_{l+1} through the identity branch with unit gain, so the training signal of deeper layers does reach shallower parameters θl\theta_{l} without attenuation. This channel, however, is parameter-level rather than activation-level, lands in layer-private parameters that only layer ll ever reads, and over the m−lm-l hops between a pair of layers l<ml<m, the deep-layer component is progressively mixed into the composite adjoint, diluted by the training signals of all intermediate layers rather than arriving at θl\theta_{l} as an isolated, addressable contribution.

Net effect. In one forward pass, a hidden state includes only earlier layers’ expert content; deeper layers’ signal reaches a shallow layer solely as a parameter update during training, never as content in its readout.

4.2 MoE with Meta Experts.

Training (write). Let yl=γ​Eθ​(x^l,R)y_{l}=\gamma E_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{l};R) and y¯l=∂ℒ/∂yl\bar{y}_{l}=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial y_{l}. Since all layers share the same pool, layer ll’s gradient contribution

gl=(∂yl∂θ)⊤​y¯l=∂ℒ∂θ|l∈ℝN​dg_{l}\;=\;\Bigl(\frac{\partial y_{l}}{\partial\theta}\Bigr)^{\!\top}\bar{y}_{l}\;=\;\left.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\theta}\right|_{l}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{Nd} (4)

accumulates with all other layers’ by the chain rule, θ¯=∑lgl\bar{\theta}=\sum_{l}g_{l} (the shared router obeys the same accumulation; we focus on the expert parameters). Thus, with learning rate η\eta, after TT training steps the storage contains the superposition of all layers’ writes:

θ(T)=θ(0)+∑l=0L−1Δ​θ¯l,Δ​θ¯l=−η∑t<Tgl(t).\theta^{(T)}\;=\;\theta^{(0)}\;+\;\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\bar{\Delta\theta}_{l},\qquad\bar{\Delta\theta}_{l}\;=\;-\eta\sum_{t<T}g_{l}^{(t)}. (5)

Equivalently, at training step tt, layer ll contributes the local parameter update Δ​θl(t)=−η​gl(t)\Delta\theta_{l}^{(t)}=-\eta g_{l}^{(t)}.

Forward (read). After training, every layer reads from the same shared expert parameters; in particular, layer mm computes ym=γ​Eθ(T)​(x^m,R)y_{m}=\gamma E_{\theta^{(T)}}(\hat{x}_{m};R). To characterize how a write from layer ll affects the readout at layer mm, we consider its local first-order effect at training step tt, evaluated at θ(t)\theta^{(t)} while holding the layer inputs fixed. Define

Jm(t)=∂Eθ​(x^m(t),R)∂θ|θ=θ(t)∈ℝH×N​d.J_{m}^{(t)}\;=\;\left.\frac{\partial E_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{m}^{(t)};R)}{\partial\theta}\right|_{\theta=\theta^{(t)}}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{H\times Nd}. (6)

Since yl=γ​Eθ​(x^l,R)y_{l}=\gamma E_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{l};R), Eq. equation 4 gives

gl(t)=γ​Jl(t)⊤​y¯l(t).g_{l}^{(t)}\;=\;\gamma{J_{l}^{(t)}}^{\top}\bar{y}_{l}^{(t)}.

Therefore, the write from layer ll at step tt induces the following first-order change in layer mm’s readout:

Δ​ym←l(t)≈γ​Jm(t)​Δ​θl(t)=−η​γ2​Jm(t)​Jl(t)⊤​y¯l(t).\Delta y_{m\leftarrow l}^{(t)}\;\approx\;\gamma J_{m}^{(t)}\Delta\theta_{l}^{(t)}\;=\;-\eta\gamma^{2}J_{m}^{(t)}{J_{l}^{(t)}}^{\top}\bar{y}_{l}^{(t)}. (7)

Accumulating these local first-order influences over training gives

ℐm←l≔∑t<TΔym←l(t)≈−ηγ2∑t<TJm(t)Jl(t)⊤y¯l(t).\mathcal{I}_{m\leftarrow l}\;\coloneqq\;\sum_{t<T}\Delta y_{m\leftarrow l}^{(t)}\;\approx\;-\eta\gamma^{2}\sum_{t<T}J_{m}^{(t)}{J_{l}^{(t)}}^{\top}\bar{y}_{l}^{(t)}. (8)

The update of the shared router contributes an analogous term, omitted because top-kk selection is piecewise constant in RR. The factor Jm(t)​Jl(t)⊤J_{m}^{(t)}{J_{l}^{(t)}}^{\top} has the form of a tangent kernel of the shared block evaluated across the two layers. The total shared-parameter influence on layer mm, ℐm=∑l=0L−1ℐm←l\mathcal{I}_{m}=\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\mathcal{I}_{m\leftarrow l}, contains contributions from every layer, in contrast to both limitations of layer-wise MoE:

  • •

    l<ml<m (deep reads shallow). Versus the frozen forward carrying of layer-wise MoE: because the write at layer ll and the readout at layer mm are two evaluations of the same operator, layer mm retrieves, re-encodes, and further transforms shallow content in the code space in which it was written.

  • •

    l>ml>m (shallow reads deep). Versus the gradient highway of layer-wise MoE: deep content reaches layer mm not as a parameter update of its private θm\theta_{m}, but as an activation-level term in its readout, in the common code space, through an O⁡(1)O(1)-length path independent of m−lm-l.

Net effect. A single forward pass provides bidirectional access along depth—deep hidden states reach shallow expert content, and shallow hidden states reach deep expert content—through one shared storage. More discussions are done in the Appendix A.4.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we present an empirical and theoretical analysis of cross-layer expert sharing in MoE models, contrasting the hierarchically arranged Local Experts of standard architectures with inter-layer shared Meta Experts. Our systematic comparisons—over the Meta/Local ratio, the activation ratio, and the topology of the shared pool—show that Meta Experts consistently reduce expert redundancy and cross-entropy loss while improving downstream task accuracy: at a fixed number of activated experts and expert granularity, models built on shared experts match the performance of Vanilla MoE with only 70–80% of the expert budget, substantially improving scaling potential. Beyond these empirical observations, our analysis shows that a shared expert block is not merely a parameter-saving device: it widens the forward residual connections and grants hidden states bidirectional access to expert content across depth, improving both the storage and the retrieval of information. Taken together, our results suggest that inter-layer redundancy, long treated as an intrinsic cost of deep MoE models, can instead be converted into effective capacity. Future directions include extending this analysis to larger models and broader architectures, and understanding why mildly hierarchical shared experts introduce redundancy without degrading performance.

AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools for writing assistance: polishing language and grammar, brainstorming alternative phrasings (e.g., for the paper title and section openings), formalizing the presentation of the theoretical analysis (e.g., LaTeX derivations whose underlying ideas are the authors’ own), and drafting descriptive passages (figure captions, the Related Work section, and the Conclusion) based on author-provided outlines, notes, and experimental results. We also used generative AI tools for code assistance, including implementation support and plotting scripts for the result figures; all designs, algorithms, and experimental ideas were proposed by the authors.

We have not used generative AI tools for research ideation, experimental design. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work: all AI-drafted text was checked, revised, and approved by the authors; translations were verified against the authors’ intended meaning; all technical claims, equations, and reported numbers were independently verified by the authors against their own derivations and experimental results; and AI-generated code was verified, tested, and debugged by the authors for correctness, with all result figures manually checked against the underlying data. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Reproducibility statement

We have taken several steps to make the results in this paper reproducible, and we reference here the parts of the paper that support them. The complete experimental configuration for the scaling ladder is given in Appendix A.3: the per-depth architecture is listed in Table 2 and the per-depth training schedule—global batch size, optimizer steps, warmup and decay, learning rate, token budget, and training FLOPs—in Table 3. Every rung, and every architectural variant at a given rung, shares the same backbone, optimizer, and parallelism policy; only the depth-dependent knobs in those tables change, so a single set of hyperparameters fully specifies each run. The evaluation protocol used for the compute-versus-loss analysis is described in the same appendix: for each run we report the language-modeling loss averaged over the final ten training steps. Our models are implemented on top of Megatron-LM, a widely used open-source framework, which helps ensure reproducibility.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Related Work

Weight Tying was originally introduced to share parameters between the embedding layer and the language model head (Press and Wolf, 2017; Inan et al., 2016): since the two matrices map tokens to and from the hidden space, tying them nearly halves the corresponding parameters while often improving perplexity, and the practice has become standard in modern language models (Vaswani et al., 2017b; Raffel et al., 2020). Beyond tying modules at the same depth, weight tying can be pushed further, to reusing parameters across depth (Dehghani et al., 2018; Lan et al., 2019).

Looped Transformer pushes weight tying to extreme: the same block is applied multiple times per token, unrolling a small set of weights into arbitrary depth (Dehghani et al., 2018; Giannou et al., 2023; Hua et al., 2025). This line of work shows that weight reuse across depth can substitute for parameter growth, and that a compact recurrent model can match the reasoning performance of much larger ones (Bae et al., 2025; Saunshi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026), at the cost of additional recursions and a higher degree of serialization. Meta Experts share the same motivation—extracting more effective capacity from a fixed parameter budget—but apply tying at a finer granularity and within a single feed-forward pass: only the expert block is reused across layers, without extra recursions, so training and inference retain the parallelism of standard Transformers, while attention may remain layer-specific. Depending on what is reused across depth, this paradigm subsumes several lines of work.

Attn Weight Sharing reuses the attention projections (or entire attention blocks) of different layers, yielding moderate parameter savings at little accuracy cost (Xiao et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2019; Mu et al., 2026). These results suggest that the per-layer parameter budget of Transformers is partially redundant—but leave open where the redundancy concentrates and whether the same principle applies to the rest of the block. Attn KV-Cache Sharing reuses not parameters but activations: in long-context or serving scenarios, multiple layers attend to a common KV cache, trading representational independence for inference memory and throughput (Sun et al., 2024; Brandon et al., 2024; Zuhri et al., 2025; Wu and Tu, 2024; Wu et al., 2025). Such sharing is typically applied at deployment time, affects the cache rather than the learned weights, and is often found to be nearly lossless—suggesting that layers can tolerate reading the same content, but not that they should store the same content. Meta Experts operate on the storage side: the shared expert pool is written by every layer during training, so cross-layer sharing reshapes what the model stores and how hidden states retrieve it, rather than merely reusing cached activations at inference.

FFN Weight Sharing is the closest line to our work: it reuses feed-forward parameters across layers, either by tying the FFN of all layers or by sharing it among a subset (Lan et al., 2019; Pires et al., 2023; Thawakar et al., 2024). Existing studies, however, focus on dense FFNs and report mixed results, and sharing is typically applied uniformly to every layer. MoE Weight Sharing has been explored in several recent works: experts are shared across layers, but almost always under an every-layer sharing topology, whose communication and memory overhead is difficult to scale (Li et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Jiao et al., 2026). Meta Experts generalize this idea to a more flexible regime: a shared pool of experts is accessed through several topology that is more friendly for communication and memory (reserving boundary layers for local experts, sub-pool partitioning with chunked or interleaved access), allows the model to decide which content is worth sharing across depth—and, as our analysis shows, implicitly turns the shared experts into bidirectional residual pathways between layers.

A.2 Redundancy Metric

To quantify how much of a model’s expert capacity is redundant, we need a measure that is (i) continuous, with no similarity threshold; (ii) comparable across architectures with different expert counts and depths; and (iii) faithful to the correlation structure among experts in high dimensions, where naive cosine similarities collapse toward zero. Our metric is built from a single similarity kernel and a single spectral statistic.

Similarity kernel: linear-CKA on centered covariances.

For expert ii, let Yi∈ℝT×HY_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times H} be its response matrix to a shared probe set of TT L2-normalized tokens, and let YicY_{i}^{c} denote YiY_{i} with its sample mean subtracted. We map each expert to the vectorized centered covariance

ϕi=vec⁡(Yic⊤​Yic),\phi_{i}\;=\;\mathrm{vec}\bigl({Y_{i}^{c}}^{\top}Y_{i}^{c}\bigr), (9)

and define the pairwise similarity as the cosine in this feature space,

Ki​j=⟨ϕi,ϕj⟩‖ϕi‖​‖ϕj‖,K_{ij}\;=\;\frac{\langle\phi_{i},\phi_{j}\rangle}{\|\phi_{i}\|\,\|\phi_{j}\|}, (10)

which is exactly linear CKA evaluated on the experts’ functional responses. Being invariant to orthogonal transformations and isotropic scaling, Ki​jK_{ij} reflects the correlated directions between experts rather than their absolute orientation or norm, and avoids the collapse of raw high-dimensional cosine. The resulting Gram matrix K∈ℝE×EK\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E} covers the EE experts under analysis: for models mixing Meta and Local Experts the two pools are concatenated on the expert axis and analyzed jointly, and for layer-wise models the layer index serves as the grouping axis.

Spectral statistic: how many directions collapse.

Since KK is positive semi-definite, its eigen-spectrum λ1≥λ2≥⋯≥λE≥0\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\dots\geq\lambda_{E}\geq 0 distributes the total similarity energy across EE principal directions. We measure the concentration of this energy by the Gini coefficient of the spectrum,

ρ=Gini⁡(λ)=∑i,j|λi−λj|2​E​∑iλi∈[0,1],\rho\;=\;\mathrm{Gini}(\lambda)\;=\;\frac{\sum_{i,j}|\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}|}{2E\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}}\;\in\;[0,1], (11)

where ρ=0\rho=0 means the energy is uniform across all directions (experts fully complementary, no redundancy) and ρ→1\rho\to 1 means it concentrates on a few directions (strong redundancy). The reading admits an exact interpretation: for a uniform rank-kk spectrum, Gini⁡(λ)=1−k/E\mathrm{Gini}(\lambda)=1-k/E, so ρ\rho equals the fraction of expert directions that have collapsed into redundant ones. Because ρ\rho is a ratio, it is directly comparable across models with different EE, depths, and training budgets, and we report it as our headline Expert Redundancy metric.

A.3 Scaling-ladder experimental settings

Models and training.

All models are trained from scratch on NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The scaling experiments use a single family of Qwen3.5-style, text-only Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models arranged as a depth-controlled ladder at four depths L∈{12,16,20,24}L\in\{12,16,20,24\}; model width is scaled jointly with depth so that each rung is (approximately) compute-optimal, giving a clean compute-versus-loss axis. At each rung, the vanilla baseline and every Meta Experts variant are trained independently, sharing the same backbone architecture and training configuration but no trained weights, and preserving the same 128×L128\times L routed-expert budget, so only the depth-dependent knobs (width, batch size, learning rate, token budget, and expert parallelism) change across rungs (Tables 2 and 3).

Each model is a hybrid-attention MoE transformer: attention layers alternate in a fixed period-4 pattern of three gated-delta-net (GDN) linear-attention layers followed by one full-attention layer, so one quarter of the layers use full softmax attention—with grouped-query attention and a head dimension of 256256—while the GDN layers use a key/value head dimension of 128128 with a depthwise causal convolution of kernel width 44. Every transformer block carries an MoE feed-forward layer with 128128 routed experts and one gated shared expert, whose intermediate widths scale with model width, and the router selects the top-88 experts per token with pre-softmax gating.

We optimize with Muon (extra scale factor 0.20.2) under a warmup–stable–decay (WSD) schedule with an inverse-square-root decay shape: the peak learning rate decreases with depth (from 1.97×10−31.97\times 10^{-3} at L=12L{=}12 to 1.278×10−31.278\times 10^{-3} at L=24L{=}24), the minimum is one tenth of the peak, warmup spans tens of steps, and the decay phase spans the final ∼10%\sim\!10\% of training; all models use a micro-batch size of 22 and a sequence length of 81928192. The reported loss is the training language-modeling loss averaged over the final ten steps, so all rungs are compared on the same quantity, and the per-rung token budget is GBS×8192×iters\mathrm{GBS}\times 8192\times\text{iters} (Table 3).

All rungs use tensor-, pipeline-, and context-parallel size 11, scaling by data and expert parallelism only: the two smaller rungs (L∈{12,16}L\in\{12,16\}) use expert-parallel size 11 with the all-gather token dispatcher, and the two larger rungs (L∈{20,24}L\in\{20,24\}) use expert-parallel size 88, the all-to-all dispatcher, and block activation recomputation on the last 44 layers, with grouped GEMM and permute fusion enabled throughout. As an illustrative parameter scale, the L=16L{=}16 vanilla backbone has ≈1.96\approx\!1.96B total parameters and ≈449\approx\!449M activated parameters per token.

Hyperparameter selection.

We do not tune the training hyperparameters per architectural variant. Instead we fix a single compute-optimal configuration for the vanilla baseline backbone at each rung and reuse it unchanged for every Meta Experts variant. The baseline configuration—the joint depth–width scaling, and the per-depth global batch size, peak learning rate, and token budget—is obtained by sweeping these settings and retaining the compute-optimal choice at each depth, following established practice on compute-optimal training and its schedule (Hoffmann et al., 2022a; Hägele et al., 2024) and on scaling laws for the learning rate and batch size (Bi et al., 2024; Team et al., 2025). The Mixture-of-Experts structural choices (expert count, granularity, and the shared-expert ratio) are likewise set in line with recent MoE scaling-law analyses (Tian et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2025). Because every Meta Experts variant inherits the baseline configuration without re-tuning, a difference in loss at a rung reflects the architectural change rather than a difference in hyperparameters; this reuse is further supported by evidence that optimal learning rate and batch size are governed primarily by the compute budget and are largely insensitive to Mixture-of-Experts architectural variation (Team et al., 2025). Moreover, at a given depth every variant keeps the per-token top-88 routing and hence the same activated parameters, and shares the same token budget, so all variants at a rung incur the same training FLOPs and are plotted at a single shared compute coordinate; the compute-versus-loss comparison at that rung is thus iso-FLOP by construction, and the only free axis across variants is the loss.

Meta Expert configurations.

Table 4 catalogues every architecture actually run in the ladder—the vanilla baseline and each model incorporating Meta Experts—each swept over all four depths L∈{12,16,20,24}L\in\{12,16,20,24\}. A Meta Expert variant changes only the routed-expert layers of the shared backbone (Table 2): it splits each layer’s 128128 routed experts into a Meta pool that is shared across depth and a set of Local experts private to that layer, and routes each token to mm meta +l+\,l local experts. We write a split as (meta width / local width) per layer; the recurring r75 base is 9696 meta / 32/\,32 local with m+l=4+4m{+}l=4{+}4. Two invariants hold for every variant at every depth and render the rungs comparable: the total routed-expert count is 128×L128\times L (iso-param, as the shared Meta pool is counted once across the LL layers) and the per-token routing is top-88 (iso-FLOP). The attention stack, gated shared expert, and training configuration are identical to the vanilla baseline, so every variant at a rung occupies the single shared compute coordinate of Table 3.

The variants span two axes. The quantitative axis is the ratio family, which varies the meta share of each layer’s 128128 experts over 25/50/75%25/50/75\%—MR25/MR50/MR75, i.e. 32/64/9632/64/96 meta with the complementary 96/64/3296/64/32 local—while routing 44 meta + 4+\,4 local per token. The topological axis fixes the r75 split and varies where and how the Meta pool is shared across depth. The first/last local-only family converts the first and last 1/2/41/2/4 layers (f1l1/f2l2/f4l4) to 128128 Local-only layers—no meta, with all 88 routed among the locals—while the interior layers retain r75; f2l2 is the F2L2 point of the main text. The meta-loop family retains r75 at every layer but replaces the single globally shared Meta pool with 2/4/82/4/8 interleaved sub-pools, each reused by every 22nd/4/4th/8/8th layer (Loop2/4/8); this tests whether Meta experts must be shared across the full depth or can instead be shared within smaller depth-local groups. The combined point F2L2++Loop2 applies both topological modifications.

The pure-Meta family removes Local experts entirely and routes the full top-88 from a single Meta pool shared across all layers (128128 per layer, 128×L128\times L in total). It constitutes the 100%100\%-meta end of the ratio axis and, like every other variant, preserves the 128×L128\times L budget and the top-88 activation.

Param-reduction ablation.

The preceding variants all fix the routed-expert budget at 128×L128\times L; the ratio family, for example, reallocates experts between meta and local within each layer’s 128128 but leaves the total unchanged. This ablation instead probes how much shared Meta capacity is required, allowing the total to fall below 128×L128\times L. Starting from the F2L2++Loop2 point, we reduce the per-layer Meta width from the r75 value of 9696 through {90,84,72,60,48}\{90,84,72,60,48\} without refilling the freed slots with Local experts. We denote each setting mplMM, for meta-per-layer width MM (Table 5).

Because only the shared Meta pool is reduced and Local is not refilled, the total routed-expert count—and hence the stored (non-embedding routed) parameters—falls below the 128×L128\times L budget, while the per-token routing remains at top-88 (44 meta + 4+\,4 local), leaving the activated experts and the training FLOPs unchanged. The sweep thus isolates a single variable, shared Meta capacity, against loss at fixed compute. It is run at all four depths, each on its standard per-depth schedule (Table 3), so the comparison remains iso-compute within every rung.

A.4 Discussion for the Residual Analysis.

Two remarks keep the claim honest. First, the path through the shared pool has O⁡(1)O(1) length—one hop from layer ll into θ\theta and one hop out to layer mm—independent of the layer distance |m−l||m-l|, whereas both pre-existing routes of layer-wise MoE (forward carrying and the gradient highway) pass through |m−l||m-l| Jacobians. The effective local gain is governed by the spectrum of the cross-layer tangent factor Jm(t)​Jl(t)⊤J_{m}^{(t)}{J_{l}^{(t)}}^{\top} appearing in Eq. equation 8; the analysis therefore characterizes access and path length, rather than guaranteeing against vanishing signals. Second, the causal direction of a single forward pass is unchanged— x^m\hat{x}_{m} does not depend on the activations of deeper layers within the same pass; what a shallow layer accesses is the content written into the shared pool by deeper layers during training. This is exactly analogous to how any trained weight carries information about the data it was trained on, with the difference that here the carrier is shared across depth, making the information accessible at every layer in a common code space.

Finally, layer-wise gradient reweighting, θ¯=∑lαl​gl\bar{\theta}=\sum_{l}\alpha_{l}g_{l} (e.g., norm equalization or conflict projection), amounts to gating this backward pathway: it modulates how much of each layer’s write Δ​θl(t)\Delta\theta_{l}^{(t)} is allowed to influence the other layers’ reads through Δ​ym←l(t)\Delta y_{m\leftarrow l}^{(t)}, and hence through the accumulated cross-layer influence ℐm←l\mathcal{I}_{m\leftarrow l}.
